lecture19.title: Neuron, Neural Networks, LLMs and Agents

sections.title: Neuron, neural networks, LLMs and agents
From a neuron to agents that communicate

teaching.text: **A neuron multiplies each input by a weight and adds the results into one response.** This inner product turns an input vector, a list of numbers, into an output that a later layer can use.
children: The small network applies this operation through layers until its final vector gives a response for each possible answer. In a vowel recognizer, those responses support a choice among vowel categories.

**A language model applies the same general idea to a sequence.** It transforms the vectors for the words already supplied and predicts probabilities for the next item. The fifteen-to-sixteen example makes the prediction target explicit.

teaching.text: **An agentic system links whole language models so they can handle different parts of a task.** An outline model plans, a writing model drafts, a critic evaluates, and a reviser responds to the critique before a final model completes the answer.
children: The critic and reviser can form a loop, while a controller directs information between models. Shared memory can keep information available across their interactions.
This graph connects complete models. Attention heads, by contrast, are processing parts inside one model.

teaching.text: **Inference uses learned weights to process an input; training changes the weights.** When a next-word prediction is wrong, backpropagation traces the error through earlier connections, and weight updates make a suitable continuation more likely.
children: Stochastic gradient descent uses these error signals to adjust weights. Running an already trained model is therefore different from training it.

teaching.text: **A language model uses layers to build representations that help predict what comes next.** Each layer transforms the vectors it receives, and later layers work with those changed representations.
children: A useful representation carries information that supports the prediction. Its values do not become useful simply by getting larger.

teaching.text: **Several attention heads contribute in parallel within one layer.** Each head learns weights that let it contribute a different view of the sequence, and the layer combines those contributions before passing the result onward.
children: Think of several experts contributing to one group decision. The experts correspond to heads, and the group corresponds to a layer.
An exam answer should distinguish parallel contributions by heads from successive transformations by layers.

teaching.text: **Attention helps connect words whose relationship matters even when other words intervene.** In “the dog that my parents ... barks,” the verb agrees with dog, not the nearer plural parents.
children: The relevant information must remain available across the intervening words. The combined head contributions help form a representation that supports this dependency.

sections.title: A dynamical rule across time and depth

teaching.text: **A dynamical system applies a rule to its current state to calculate a new state.** In the oscillator, position changes using velocity, then velocity changes using the new position.
children: With initial position one and velocity zero, position first stays still. The positive position makes velocity negative; that negative velocity then carries position downward. Repeating the updates produces the trajectory.

teaching.text: **A recurrent network carries information forward through feedback.** Plan and state units feed a hidden layer, whose output returns to the state units.
children: Self-connections preserve a fading trace of the earlier state. The same weights are reused at each moment, so recent output can affect what comes next.

teaching.text: **Depth plays the role of successive moments in the language-model comparison.** Each layer transforms the representation from the layer before it, so values develop along a path through the network.
children: The oscillator and recurrent network reuse one rule over time. Different language-model layers can have different weights, even though each stage depends on the state produced before it.

sections.title: One prediction task for different sequences

teaching.text: **A model can predict the next item in different kinds of sequences.** Fifteen input vectors can stand for fifteen words, sound frames, picture patches or amino acids; the model then predicts item sixteen.
children: In “The cat that the dog chased ran up the old tree and sat on the ___,” the sentence’s relationships indicate that the cat is the one that sat.

A spectrogram represents successive sound frames, with the next frame predicted after the supplied sequence. A four-by-four picture has sixteen patches; after fifteen are supplied, the missing patch is at bottom right.
The insulin B-chain example supplies fifteen amino acids and predicts Y as the following residue.

teaching.text: **The input format is shared, but the vectors represent different information.** Sound frames unfold over time, picture patches follow a reading order, and amino acids follow positions in a chain.
children: Using vectors gives the model a numerical sequence to process. It does not make sound, images, words and proteins the same kind of data.

sections.title: Which sequences can be English words?

teaching.text: **Phonotactics is knowledge of which sound sequences a language permits.** An English syllable can follow a consonant-vowel-consonant pattern, as in mat or fish.
children: The pattern concerns sounds rather than letters. The final e in shave is silent, while two letters can spell one consonant sound, as in ship.

teaching.text: **English consonant clusters have restrictions on their order.** A cluster before the vowel is an onset, as in split; a cluster after it is a coda, as in help.
children: Flat places l next to the vowel, while the starred form *lfat reverses the onset order. Help places l next to the vowel before p; *hepl reverses the coda order.
Other languages allow different sequences. Russian permits initial clusters such as zb, while Spanish may place a vowel before an initial s-plus-consonant sequence.

teaching.text: **Syllable boundaries affect which sound sequences are possible.** The t and l in At-lan-tic can occur across a syllable break, while *tlantic begins with a cluster English does not allow.
children: Likewise, ng can end a syllable, as in ring, but it cannot start one in the English examples. A sequence’s position in the word matters.

sections.title: Guessing the next letter reveals phonotactic knowledge

teaching.text: **A next-letter prediction task can test whether a model learns sound and spelling patterns.** A beginning such as ra allows many continuations, while the start skr permits only a vowel in the examples.
children: After sp, l, r or a vowel can follow, but *spn does not fit. After k, a vowel or n can follow, as in knee; after sh, a vowel or r can follow, as in shrimp.
The probabilities form a distribution over possible next letters. A broad set of plausible continuations spreads probability, while a restricted onset concentrates it.

teaching.text: **A small language model can be trained to predict the next letter from English word patterns.** The described design uses four heads in each of five layers, 64 numbers per token vector, and 1,000 randomly selected English words.
children: The model predicts from the letters already supplied and updates its weights after an error. Ten generated examples after each step provide samples of its current output.
A pronunciation lexicon can guide learning toward word sounds rather than treating every written letter as a separate sound.

teaching.text: **The initial output remained largely gibberish, so the run did not establish successful syllable learning.** Some vowel-like forms were only a tentative observation.
children: Training on 10,000 words and running more iterations were proposed extensions. They are possible next steps, not evidence of a successful result.

An agentic system can use an English instruction to build and run the smaller model. NumPy and a pronunciation resource were reported as implementation components; the larger system’s abilities do not mean the new model already knows English.
Shannon’s earlier statistical examples show how adding constraints makes letter sequences more English-like. They illustrate sequence structure, not modern attention-based architecture.

sections.title: Design an agentic system for English syllables

teaching.text: **An LLM learns by guessing a hidden word from the words before it.** In “The chef cracks the,” each earlier word is a clue about the word that follows.
children: The relationships between the clue words and the hidden word are **interdependencies**.

teaching.text: **The model spreads its bets because it does not know the answer.** It bets most on “egg,” less on “nut” and least on “code.”
children: Learning nudges the weights so that the right word gets a bigger bet next time.

teaching.text: **The same learning applies when the signal holds sounds and images.** The model still guesses a hidden piece from the other pieces.
children: Only the content of the signal is different.

sections.title: Text, speech and images in three different forms

teaching.text: **Text already comes as a row of pieces, so each piece can become a vector.** That makes text easy for the model to read.
children: Speech is air pressure changing in time, and an image is a grid of light.

teaching.text: **Speech and images contain no words.** They are not rows of pieces when they arrive.
children: An LLM can read only a row of vectors.

teaching.text: **Speech and images therefore have to be converted into rows of vectors.** The conversion is the first job.
children: After it, all three forms can be read by one model.

sections.title: Speech becomes a row of frame vectors

teaching.text: **Speech is cut into slices of about 20 milliseconds, and each slice is a frame.** The slices follow one another in time.
children: A speech encoder, which is a network trained on a large amount of audio, changes each slice into a vector.

teaching.text: **One vector comes out for each slice.** Different sounds give different numbers in the vector.
children: The vectors stay in time order.

teaching.text: **One second of speech becomes 50 vectors.** The speech is now a row, just like a sentence.
children: The LLM can read that row one vector after another.

sections.title: Images become a row of patch vectors

teaching.text: **An image is cut into small squares called patches.** The egg image is cut into 16 patches.
children: The patches are laid out in a row in reading order, so the image becomes a sequence.

teaching.text: **A vision encoder gives one vector for each patch.** The 16 patches become 16 vectors in the same order.
children: The image is now a row that the LLM can read.

teaching.text: **Real systems use much smaller patches of 14 to 16 pixels.** One image then gives hundreds of vectors.
children: Smaller patches mean more patches for the same image.

teaching.text: **Image patches, speech frames and words are placed in one row.** The last word after “Now crack the” is hidden.
children: The earlier words still give clues about the hidden word.

teaching.text: **A patch containing an egg and the sound of cracking also give clues.** A clue that crosses from one sense to another is a **cross-modal dependency**.
children: These clues are added to the clues from the words.

teaching.text: **The game is the same as with text alone.** The model guesses the hidden piece from the other pieces.
children: The difference is that some clues now come from other senses.

sections.title: Three cute puppies as an image, speech and words

teaching.text: **“Three cute puppies” appears as an image, as speech and as written words.** The image is cut into 18 patches.
children: The speech is a spectrogram, where time runs left to right, higher means higher frequency and darker means more energy.

teaching.text: **Each thin column of the spectrogram is one frame.** The three words follow one another in time.
children: The written words are the third form of the same phrase.

teaching.text: **The three forms are three views of one event.** Training places all three in one row.
children: The model then guesses whichever piece of the row is hidden.

sections.title: Training example 1 predicts the next word

teaching.text: **With the words “three cute” alone, the model’s bets are spread out.** “Kittens,” “puppies” and “babies” all fit.
children: No single word is far ahead of the others.

teaching.text: **With the image and the sound, the bet piles up on “puppies.”** The image contains puppies, and the sound contains the spoken word.
children: These are clues from the other senses.

teaching.text: **The model bet 0.85 on the true word, so the error is small.** A small error gives a small nudge to the weights.
children: A large bet on the truth leaves little to correct.

sections.title: Training example 2 predicts a sound frame

teaching.text: **The model can be trained to predict a hidden frame of sound.** The sound is predicted frame by frame from left to right.
children: The earlier frames help because the voice and the formants change smoothly.

teaching.text: **The words say which sound comes next, and here it is the vowel in “pup.”** The image contains puppies, so it backs up the words.
children: The image is the weaker clue in this case.

teaching.text: **A frame is a column of numbers for the energy in each frequency band.** The error is how far the guessed numbers are from the true numbers.
children: That error nudges the weights.

sections.title: Training example 3 predicts an image patch

teaching.text: **The model can be trained to predict a hidden patch of the image.** The patches are predicted in reading order.
children: The earlier patches give background above and two puppies to the left.

teaching.text: **“Three” says a third puppy must appear, and “puppies” says to expect dog ears.** The sound carries the same words as a backup.
children: These clues give the content of the patch.

teaching.text: **The guess is a puppy ear in the average colour of the first two puppies, but the true puppy is dark.** The biggest error is the colour, because no clue gave it.
children: Only systems that also produce images are trained this way.

sections.title: Every piece can be the hidden one

teaching.text: **A hidden word, a hidden frame and a hidden patch each get a clue from every sense.** For a hidden word, the clues are a plural noun, the word just spoken, and puppies in the image.
children: The other two cases work the same way with their own clues.

teaching.text: **A clue from the same sense says how the signal continues.** Grammar, smooth formants, and fur and background are the three examples.
children: Each one carries on from what came before in its own sense.

teaching.text: **Clues from the other senses say what the thing is.** Here the thing is puppies, three of them.
children: Training on all three senses together helps because each sense fills gaps the others leave.

sections.title: Talking back, and what is new

teaching.text: **To speak, the model predicts codes for sound.** Sound is compressed into discrete codes that work like new words in the vocabulary.
children: The next code is predicted like the next word.

teaching.text: **A decoder changes the codes back into sound.** The result is a sound wave that can be heard.
children: The model predicts the codes, and the decoder makes the sound.

teaching.text: **Three things are new, which are a shared currency of vectors in one row, data where the senses appear together, and a schedule that protects what was already learned.** These make training on three senses possible.
children: What stays the same is finding the dependencies in the signal.
